meta.title: Hungarian Alphabet
meta.subtitle: The 44 letters and their sounds, then stress and doubled letters (46 notes) · both directions, as two cards each
meta.desc: The Hungarian alphabet and its sounds: 46 notes — the forty-four letters in Hungarian alphabetical order, capital and small, with each one's Hungarian name; then two notes on what no single letter shows, the stress and the doubled consonant. The first deck of the Hungarian collection. Hungarian uses the Latin alphabet, but its letters do not say what they say in English — s is "sh", sz is "s", c is "ts", a is close to the o of British hot — and nine of its letters are written with two or three characters (cs, dz, dzs, gy, ly, ny, sz, ty, zs), each a letter in its own right. The accents are part of the letter: á, é, í, ó and ú are long vowels, and the double accent of ő and ű marks a long ö and ü. Both directions: see a letter and recall its sound, or see a sound and recall the letter, each a card with its own schedule. Every note describes the sound in English words and gives one everyday word that shows it, with a speaker beside the letter and the word. j and ly are the same sound, so each note says which spelling it is; q, w, x and y belong to the alphabet but are met only in loanwords and names, and their notes say so. The sounds are approximations, as every learner's alphabet gives them; where English has no equivalent — ö, ü, gy, ty — the card says what to do instead. Sources: the standard description of Hungarian spelling and pronunciation; the example words are checked against English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0).

fields.Name: a
fields.Sound: a short "o" as in British hot, said with the lips a little rounded — never the a of cat

fields.Name: á
fields.Sound: a long, open "a" as in father

fields.Name: bé
fields.Sound: "b" as in bed

fields.Name: cé
fields.Sound: "ts" as in cats — never a k or an s

fields.Name: csé
fields.Sound: "ch" as in church

fields.Name: dé
fields.Sound: "d" as in dog

fields.Name: dzé
fields.Sound: "dz" as in adze — a d and a z said as one sound, often held long between vowels

fields.Name: dzsé
fields.Sound: "j" as in jam — mostly in words from other languages

fields.Name: e
fields.Sound: "e" as in bed, said with the mouth more open, nearly the a of cat

fields.Name: é
fields.Sound: "ay" as in say, but long and steady, with no glide into "ee"

fields.Name: ef
fields.Sound: "f" as in fun

fields.Name: gé
fields.Sound: "g" as in go — always hard, also before e and i

fields.Name: gyé
fields.Sound: a "d" and a "y" run together into one sound, as in British duke or dew

fields.Name: há
fields.Sound: "h" as in hat; silent at the end of a word (méh, "bee")

fields.Name: i
fields.Sound: "ee" as in see, but short

fields.Name: í
fields.Sound: "ee" as in see, long

fields.Name: jé
fields.Sound: "y" as in yes — j, the usual spelling of this sound

fields.Name: ká
fields.Sound: "k" as in skin, without a puff of breath

fields.Name: el
fields.Sound: "l" as in leaf, always clear

fields.Name: elipszilon
fields.Sound: "y" as in yes — ly, an old spelling of the same sound as j, kept in certain words (hely, folyó, király) and learnt with each

fields.Name: em
fields.Sound: "m" as in man

fields.Name: en
fields.Sound: "n" as in net

fields.Name: eny
fields.Sound: "ny" as in canyon — an n and a y run together into one sound, like Spanish ñ

fields.Name: o
fields.Sound: a short, closed "o", lips rounded — a pure vowel, not the "ow" of English go

fields.Name: ó
fields.Sound: the same closed "o", long, still with no glide into "w"

fields.Name: ö
fields.Sound: the German ö or the French eu: say "e" as in bed with the lips rounded — short

fields.Name: ő
fields.Sound: the same rounded "ö", long — the double accent marks a long ö

fields.Name: pé
fields.Sound: "p" as in spin, without a puff of breath

fields.Name: kú
fields.Sound: a "k" — only in foreign names and a few loanwords

fields.Name: er
fields.Sound: a rolled or tapped "r", as in Spanish or Scottish English

fields.Name: es
fields.Sound: "sh" as in ship — never the s of see

fields.Name: esz
fields.Sound: "s" as in see

fields.Name: té
fields.Sound: "t" as in stop, without a puff of breath

fields.Name: tyé
fields.Sound: a "t" and a "y" run together into one sound, as in British tune

fields.Name: u
fields.Sound: "oo" as in book, short, lips rounded

fields.Name: ú
fields.Sound: "oo" as in food, long

fields.Name: ü
fields.Sound: the German ü or the French u: say "ee" with the lips rounded — short

fields.Name: ű
fields.Sound: the same rounded "ü", long — the double accent marks a long ü

fields.Name: vé
fields.Sound: "v" as in van

fields.Name: dupla vé
fields.Sound: a "v" — only in foreign names and a few loanwords

fields.Name: iksz
fields.Sound: "ks" as in box — in loanwords

fields.Name: ipszilon
fields.Sound: an "ee", written as a letter of its own only in old family names; everywhere else y is the second half of gy, ly, ny and ty
fields.Example: Adya family name (Endre Ady, the poet)

fields.Name: zé
fields.Sound: "z" as in zoo

fields.Name: zsé
fields.Sound: "s" as in pleasure — the French j

fields.Name: hangsúly
fields.Sound: the stress: every word is stressed on its FIRST syllable, whatever its length — an accent mark never shows stress, only a long vowel (KÁ-vé)

fields.Name: kettőzött mássalhangzó
fields.Sound: a doubled consonant is held for longer (itt, "here", is "it-t", as in cat tail); a doubled two-letter consonant doubles only its first letter (sz + sz is ssz: asszony)
